History:
• Chief complaint: Wheezing and shortness of breath for ~2 days.  
• Onset/trigger: Began about 1 h after heavy house-cleaning with exposure to dust.  
• Course: Persistent; subjectively getting worse, particularly at night; now interfering with speaking (cannot complete sentences at times).  
• Associated symptoms: No chest pain on deep inspiration, no dizziness, no syncope. Hydration adequate (≈4–5 glasses water/day).  
• Interventions tried: None; has an inhaler from “a couple of months ago” but has not used it for this episode.  
• Relevant history: Childhood asthma (occasional exercise-induced symptoms in adulthood); seasonal hay fever. Prior courses of oral steroids for asthma (dates/doses unspecified).  

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (childhood, intermittent in adulthood).  
• Allergic rhinitis/hay fever.  
• No other chronic illnesses mentioned.  
Allergies:
• No known drug or other allergies reported.  
Medications:
• Asthma inhaler (exact drug/dose/route/frequency not documented, last used “a couple of months ago”).  
• No regular antihistamine; none currently at home.  
• No other medications stated.  

Physical Examination:
(Tele-consult; no direct vitals obtained)  
• General: Conversing, alert, oriented, but reports dyspnea and audible wheeze.  
• Respiratory: Subjective wheeze, worse at night; denies pleuritic pain.  
• Cardiovascular/Neuro: Denies dizziness, syncope.  
• No signs of acute distress reported beyond shortness of breath.  

Impression:
Probable asthma exacerbation versus dust-induced allergic airway reaction.

Management Plan:
• Advise immediate in-person review at local GP/clinic for objective assessment: pulse oximetry, peak flow, and further examination.  
• Obtain over-the-counter antihistamine en route (or have GP prescribe) to address possible allergic component.  
• Possible need for short course of oral steroids and/or updated inhaler regimen—decision deferred to in-person assessment.  
• Clinician to provide written referral/summary letter via app for patient to present to GP.  
• Emergency precautions discussed (seek urgent care if worsening breathlessness, inability to speak, chest tightness, or lips/fingers turning blue).  

Patient Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma now presents with 2-day history of worsening wheeze and dyspnea after dust exposure while cleaning. No chest pain or dizziness. Differential favors an asthma flare triggered by dust allergy. She is directed to obtain antihistamine and attend GP today for objective evaluation and potential steroids.

Key Takeaways:
• Buy and take a single antihistamine tablet today if available.  
• Go to GP/clinic today for oxygen saturation check and asthma assessment.  
• Seek emergency help if breathing worsens, speech becomes difficult, or cyanosis develops.

Next Steps:
• In-person GP visit with pulse oximetry, peak flow, and respiratory exam.  
• Update/renew inhaler prescription and consider oral steroids based on findings.  
• Consider formal allergy evaluation and asthma action plan at follow-up.
